title: The Hero Isn't Always the One With the Sword
author: Jennifer Haber
summary: A seventh-grade English teacher explains why she opens every school year with a ten-day Hero's Journey unit built entirely on wordless, six-to-eight-minute short films rather than a familiar sword-and-monster movie, and argues the unit's real purpose is teaching character analysis rather than plot recognition. Drawing on Joseph Campbell's twelve-stage framework, she reframes 'hero' away from combat and toward ordinary people facing unfamiliar difficulty, which she says gives students a far more specific vocabulary for character change than the usual vague answer that a character 'learned to be brave.' The choice of dialogue-free films like Piper, Hair Love, and Paperman is deliberate: because no language barrier gates entry, students two years below and two years above grade level can argue the same interpretive questions on equal footing, and groups routinely rewatch scenes to defend competing readings of where the ordeal or the mentor moment actually falls. The unit's payoff, she argues, is durable: once students have shared vocabulary for the twelve stages, that vocabulary becomes the analytic lens applied to every subsequent text the class reads that year, from Gilgamesh through the final spring novel.
points: Framing the unit around ordinary, non-heroic protagonists (a frightened bird, a father doing his daughter's hair) rather than a sword-and-monster narrative deliberately breaks students' assumption that the 'hero' must be the strongest character, redirecting attention to how anyone responds to difficulty.

Using wordless short films is a specific pedagogical design choice, not just a hook: without dialogue to lean on, a student two years below grade level can analyze character on equal footing with one two years above, since evidence must come from expression and action alone.

The Hero's Journey vocabulary becomes a durable shared language that persists across the entire school year -- a student can say a character 'refused the call' in April and the class understands instantly, because the same twelve-stage framework is reapplied to every subsequent text.

Group disagreement about where a story's true ordeal falls is treated as the pedagogical payoff, not a failure of consensus -- students must return to specific frames of the film to defend competing stage-placements with evidence.
quotes: But most heroes don't begin as heroes. They begin as ordinary people facing something they don't yet know how to face. Once students understand that, they stop looking for the sword or the monster and start looking at what the character does when something becomes difficult.
A seventh grader who has just finished a book often doesn't know where to begin, and the answer usually ends up somewhere near 'she learned to be brave.

Students who have never willingly reread a paragraph will rewatch a scene six times because they want to prove their interpretation. A student reading two years below grade level can analyze the same story as a student reading two years above it because difficult language isn't keeping them out of the discussion.

A student in the middle of the year can say that a character has refused the call, or that this is the moment the character meets the mentor, and the rest of the class knows exactly what they mean.
I also want students to see that heroes can be ordinary people. Very few of them will ever fight a monster, but every one of them will face something they don't know how to handle.
